newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COFFEE -- Brazil needs production boost for future.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE -- Brazil needs production boost for future.

text.p: Rising internal demand in Brazil may mean Brazilian coffee production will have to rise to 30 million to 35 million 60-kg bags by the year 2000 if it wishes to maintain its international market share, traders said.

The idea of a 35 million bag crop was not regarded as ridiculous by traders and producers attending a seminar this week in Espirito Santo, said Frederico Daher, superintendent of the state's Coffee Technology Center.
"People were saying that a crop of 35 million bags in the future is not an exaggeration," Daher said.

However some traders are concerned that a period of low international prices combined with adverse weather conditions has left Brazilian production at a critical point from which it can only recover if prices rise.
"The low prices seen in 1989 to 1992 together with the 1994 frosts and drought have jeopardised the financial status of the sector," said Francisco Ourique of Flavour Coffee.
"Coffee production will need to go up and the only way this can happen is either with higher prices or a change in the exchange rate..It is a bomb waiting to explode," he said.

According to the Brazilian Coffee Industry Association (ABIC) which represents roasters, internal coffee consumption this year should reach 11 million bags against 10.1 million bags in 1995 and 6.4 million bags in 1985.
ABIC hopes domestic roastings will grow further to 15 million bags by the year 2000, of which up to 500,000 could actually be exported, said ABIC secretary-general David Nahum.
As for exports of beans, under an accord agreed with members of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries, Brazil should ship 15 million bags in the July/June 1996/97 crop year.

Exporters would like to maintain this level in the coming years but this means that with the growing internal demand and also allowing for soluble coffee, Brazil needs to see production of around 35 million bags by early next century.
"We do not want to see internal demand growing at the expense of exporters, we also want exports to rise," said Nahum.
"Therefore we have an eventual production goal of 35 million to 40 million bags," he added.

Brazil's crop is still showing the impact of the 1994 frosts and drought, with a 1996/97 harvest of around 25 million to 27 million bags and producers already anticipating a smaller crop in 1997/1998 due to tree stress in some areas.

Many in the international market however appear to be expecting a larger Brazilian crop in 1997/98 and some even believe that the crop that has just been harvested is bigger than current forecasts, Ourique said.

"People think selling pressure in the past two weeks from Brazil is because the crop is larger but producers in fact are selling so that they can repay loans to the Banco do Brasil due by October 30," he said.
In terms of increasing production, there is no shortage of area which can be used for new coffee production but for traders and producers the key is productivity.
"We don't want to increase planted area but instead improve productivity with new technology," Daher said.
One possible problem is that the key producing areas have moved north from the traditional regions of Parana and Sao Paulo, Ourique said.

"The more further north the Brazilian frontier of production moves, the more capital sensitive it becomes. We are coming out of the naturally rich soils of Parana and Sao Paulo to the lower quality soils of regions such as the Cerrado," Ourique said.
"There if the cost of production is not covered, farmers won't use fertilizers and in regions like this, if I don't use fertilizers, then output can drop up to 50 percent," he added.
-- Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
